comparator.name: Ancient Studies
comparator.institution: University of Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
comparator.sourceNotes: The joint degree combines interdisciplinary Ancient Studies with one required specialisation. This example selects Ancient History, the broad historical direction and first-listed specialisation in the adopted regulations, before considering UCR. It includes Classical Mythology and Seminar Ancient History as the two orientation choices, five named specialisation courses, 30 EC open space and a 12 EC thesis including the thesis colloquium. All three years total 60 EC.
components: Objects in Context: An Interdisciplinary Perspective on the Ancient World
The Academic Literacy Test, ACASA orientation and tutoring support carry no credits. Writing support is provided when the diagnostic test indicates it is needed.
The Classical Canon 1: The Heritage of Antiquity
A Cultural History of the Ancient World 1: The Near East and the Greek World
A Cultural History of the Ancient World 2: The Hellenistic World, Italy and Rome
This orientation seminar follows the two first-year cultural-history surveys and prepares for Ancient History. Seminar participation is compulsory.
Entry requires both first-year Cultural History of the Ancient World courses, or equivalent introductory study.
Students prepare and carry out an interdisciplinary excursion research project. Practical exercises require at least 85% attendance under the programme regulations.
Past and Present: Critical Approaches to Antiquity and Archaeological Heritage
The Classical Canon 2: The Sociology of Cultural Selection
History and Culture of the Ancient Near East
The Decline and Fall of Rome
Politics and International Relations in Antiquity

The 30 EC elective period may include a minor, approved study abroad or a placement of up to 12 EC. Normally no more than 12 EC may be introductory, and at least 24 EC must be outside the programme. Approved exceptions apply to specified minors and language sequences.
In Search of the Masses of Antiquity
The 12 EC thesis includes the thesis colloquium. Students must pass all first- and second-year courses before starting. They conduct individual interdisciplinary research under supervision.

routeSelection.basis: The generic merged target includes Dutch and English delivery. The English Ancient Studies track represents its international academic identity. Ancient History is the broad historical specialisation rather than a specific language or material-method route and is also first in Article 10.2 and the specialisation table. The selection precedes UCR implementation.

core: Interdisciplinary interpretation of ancient textual, visual and material sources
Ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern histories, societies and political systems
Ancient art, literature, mythology, philosophy and religion
Cultural contact and comparison across the ancient Mediterranean and Western Asia
Ancient Near Eastern Studies, Greek and Latin specialisation choices, with acknowledged UCR language-depth limits
Humanities methods, source criticism, academic writing and independent interdisciplinary research
adjacent: Archaeology, material culture, museums and classical heritage
Reception of antiquity, canon formation and public memory
Ancient history, democracy, political thought and rhetoric
questions: How can texts, objects and sites be combined to reconstruct ancient societies?
How did cultural contact shape ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern worlds?
How are antiquity, heritage and political ideas selected and reinterpreted in the present?

trace: develops academic writing, literature evaluation, reflective practice and civic research skills
introduces legal traditions, social justice and legal reasoning as modern analytical perspectives on institutions and their historical interpretation
examines modern transformations and historical visions of the future, supporting study of how later societies frame and reuse the past
compares ancient Persia, Rome and China with later empires through institutions, legitimacy, cultural power and historical evidence
traces warfare from antiquity onward, using strategic texts and primary sources to test claims about Western power

develops historical research questions, source criticism and an independent paper in the American context; its contribution is historical method rather than ancient regional content

develops interpretation and evaluation of ethical theories, including ancient virtue ethics and later reinterpretations
examines historical and contemporary theories of emotion and their place in ethics, politics and art, supporting interpretation of cultural and philosophical texts
studies political thought from classical antiquity onward through original texts and historically situated arguments
develops empirical comparison of political institutions and democracy, complementing historical interpretations of ancient political communities
provides competing theories of interstate relations and case-based interpretation, complementing ancient conflict and political history without substituting for its sources
examines conflict, colonial legacies, identity and peacebuilding with interdisciplinary methods, providing a critical comparative perspective on political memory
examines social identities, boundaries, inequality and institutions, supporting interpretation of social groups and cultural selection
develops interviews, documentary inquiry, qualitative interpretation and reflexivity for research on public memory and cultural institutions
studies Greek and Roman rhetorical traditions and practices analysis of arguments and public speech
develops close linguistic and stylistic analysis of literary and non-fiction texts
studies persuasion, framing and ethical communication and tests public-facing interpretations through community projects
develops poetry, creative forms, revision and critically justified artistic choices, supporting the public and creative reception of cultural narratives
develops close visual analysis and contextual interpretation of Western art from the Renaissance onward, supporting comparison of later artistic traditions and heritage
interprets artefacts, technologies and craft organisation from the Neolithic through antiquity and practises archaeological recording and inference
examines African artistic traditions, colonial collecting and restitution, providing comparative analysis of heritage ownership and museum conflict
examines Renaissance Italian art and cross-Mediterranean exchange as a later cultural setting for interpreting classical legacies
studies material evidence of community and democracy in ancient Greece
examines museums, display choices and critical narratives of modern art, complementing the study of canon formation and public heritage
combines ancient Athenian history, archaeology, literature, religion and material sources to investigate democracy, exclusion and its modern uses
studies the history and methods of art history through influential texts and arguments about interpretation and cultural context
develops close reading, practical criticism and analysis of narrative, poetry and drama
compares ancient epic and Greek tragedy with later works through literary form, recurring motifs and cultural context
compares Greek, Roman, Near Eastern and other mythic traditions and their transmission, including creative reinterpretation of Ovid
studies adaptation, intertextuality and changes between literary narrative and film as methods for analysing reception
applies humanist, feminist, Marxist and other perspectives to literary meaning and research
develops formal and critical analysis of moving-image representation, supporting public presentation and interpretation of the past
examines media objects and infrastructures as material sources shaping knowledge and memory, a comparative material-culture method
studies racial construction, exclusion and marginalized storytelling through archives, media and participant inquiry, supporting critical reflection on cultural representation
develops documentary analysis and production, including research, interviewing and ethical choices in public representation

alternatives.label: Ancient worlds: texts, objects & ideas
alternatives.concept: Study ancient cultures through objects, texts and ideas, then investigate how later societies interpret them. Combine world and Greek archaeology, ancient democracy, literature and myth, philosophy, rhetoric and historical research.
alternatives.labelReason: Study ancient cultures through objects, texts and ideas, then investigate how later societies interpret them. Combine world and Greek archaeology, ancient democracy, literature and myth, philosophy, rhetoric and historical research.
progression: Checked every formal prerequisite and offered term in the current workbook. Foundational archaeology precedes advanced ancient-democracy study; introductory literary and historical work supports advanced interpretation and research.

alternatives.label: Archaeology, heritage & public memory
alternatives.concept: Study material culture and public memory through archaeology, art history, museums and historical inquiry. Compare the interpretation and public presentation of ancient heritage with later histories and collections.
alternatives.labelReason: Study material culture and public memory through archaeology, art history, museums and historical inquiry. Compare the interpretation and public presentation of ancient heritage with later histories and collections.
alternatives.distinctness: This option gives sustained weight to museum practices, art and heritage, documentary work, public history and cultural representation. The closest option places more weight on textual interpretation, philosophy and creative writing.
progression: Checked every formal prerequisite and offered term in the current workbook. Foundational archaeology precedes advanced ancient-democracy study; introductory literary and historical work supports advanced interpretation and research.

alternatives.label: Ancient worlds, political ideas & reception
alternatives.concept: Study ancient political ideas and institutions alongside their later interpretation. Combine Greek archaeology and democracy, histories of empire and warfare, political philosophy, myth, cultural history and methods for analysing historical and contemporary political evidence.
alternatives.labelReason: Study ancient political ideas and institutions alongside their later interpretation. Combine Greek archaeology and democracy, histories of empire and warfare, political philosophy, myth, cultural history and methods for analysing historical and contemporary political evidence.
alternatives.distinctness: This option prioritises political thought, institutions, rights, conflicts and comparative history. Both ancient material evidence and modern political methods are present; it does not claim a specialist ancient-history degree.
progression: Checked every formal prerequisite and offered term in the current workbook. Foundational archaeology precedes advanced ancient-democracy study; introductory literary and historical work supports advanced interpretation and research.

selection.assessment: The closest option implements a balanced ancient material, textual and intellectual core. Archaeology and public memory and political history and reception are coherent target-supported priorities, with substantive curricular consequences. Each pair passes the thirty-EC floor. Language-specific directions remain acknowledged limitations rather than weak separate programmes. Three is the maximum.

blocks: Both interpret material objects as evidence of past societies and develop archaeological documentation and inference.
Both investigate contested heritage, ownership and public narratives; UCR focuses on African art, colonial collections and restitution rather than the UNESCO framework.
Both examine later cultural uses and transformations of classical heritage; UCR concentrates on Renaissance visual culture and its wider connections.
Both use material evidence to study ancient Greek communities; the external survey also covers the Near East and a longer chronology.
Both examine cultural selection and the institutions and narratives that make works canonical; UCR focuses on modern art and museums.
Both examine participation, social groups and exclusion in ancient political life using textual and material evidence; UCR concentrates on Athens.
Both examine disciplinary methods, knowledge and interpretation in the humanities; UCR focuses on art history.
Ancient history, society and political systems
Both investigate empire, political power and decline with historical sources; UCR compares Rome with other ancient and later empires.
Both use theories of interstate relations to interpret political conflict; UCR uses modern cases while the external course works directly from ancient evidence.
Both develop interpretation of ancient philosophical arguments; UCR extends into later and contemporary philosophy.
Both interpret influential ancient literary works and their cultural significance; UCR also compares later works.
Both study Greek and Roman myth, its transmission and cultural interpretation; UCR compares further traditions.
Rhetoric, methods, research and choice space
Both develop creative writing, revision and critical justification of forms for a wider audience; UCR is not restricted to classical reception.

notes.text: The joint UvA–VU degree combines ancient textual and material sources with a required specialisation, excursion and thesis. This example follows Ancient History. UCR offers related study in archaeology, myth, philosophy, heritage and historical interpretation, but does not reproduce the full ancient-history sequence or provide Greek, Latin or Akkadian language sequences.

audience.programmeDescription: Ancient Studies is a joint UvA–VU degree combining the history, texts, objects and ideas of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East. Students study cultural interaction and the later uses of antiquity, then complete a specialisation and interdisciplinary thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options connect archaeology, ancient democracy, literature, myth and philosophy with historical and cultural interpretation. The joint degree offers a more sustained ancient-world curriculum, a required specialisation and an excursion. This comparison uses its English-taught Ancient History route.
